sections.title: Step 11 — Interview Preparation
sections.body:
### A. Conceptual Interview Questions

**Q1: How does Neo4j handle read scaling in a production GraphRAG system?**
> **Answer:** Neo4j scales reads via **causal clustering**: a primary server handles all writes, and 1-N read replicas serve read queries (graph traversals). The primary asynchronously replicates the transaction log to replicas. For GraphRAG: ~95% of operations are reads (traversal queries), so replicas handle most load. Load balancing strategy: use **bookmark-based causal consistency** — after a write, the client holds a bookmark that ensures subsequent reads see that write. For GraphRAG production: queries go to read replicas via load balancer (round-robin or least-connections). Writes (new entity/relationship insertions) go to primary. Replica lag: typically < 1 second, occasionally 2-3 seconds during heavy write bursts. If the system requires that queries ALWAYS see the latest graph state (e.g., after real-time ingestion), route to primary. Otherwise, accept replica lag for better throughput.

**Q2: Why is cache warming critical for GraphRAG production systems?**
> **Answer:** GraphRAG's graph traversal queries are expensive (50-200ms each), but results for popular entities are extremely repetitive — "Apple Inc", "Microsoft", "OpenAI" appear in thousands of queries daily. Without cache warming: after a deployment or cache flush, every request for popular entities hits Neo4j simultaneously → cache stampede → Neo4j CPU spikes → all users experience high latency (3-8 seconds instead of 100ms). Cache warming: before enabling the load balancer health check (before accepting traffic), pre-load top-K entity neighborhoods into Redis. Determine top-K from: production query analytics (entity frequency over past 7 days). Cache warm time: 1000 entities × 50ms per Neo4j query = 50 seconds. Then: enable health check → load balancer routes traffic → first users see cached responses. This reduces P95 latency during cache miss from 3s to 100ms.

**Q3: When should you use a message queue (Kafka) for GraphRAG ingestion vs. synchronous ingestion?**
> **Answer:** Synchronous ingestion: document arrives → extract entities → update graph immediately → confirm. Problem: NER + LLM extraction takes 5-20 seconds per document. If 10,000 documents arrive in a batch, synchronous = hours of blocking, no retry mechanism, single point of failure. Kafka-based ingestion: documents published to Kafka topic → multiple Celery/worker processes consume → each worker extracts entities → writes to Neo4j. Benefits: (1) Decoupling: ingestion speed independent of consumer speed; (2) Retry: failed messages reprocessed; (3) Backpressure: Kafka buffers documents during spikes; (4) Scaling: add workers without changing producer; (5) Durability: messages persisted for configured retention period. Rule: use Kafka when ingestion volume > processing capacity, or when ingestion and indexing must be decoupled. For < 10 docs/minute: synchronous is fine. For 10+ docs/minute or burst patterns: Kafka.

**Q4: What is a circuit breaker and why is it essential for production GraphRAG?**
> **Answer:** A circuit breaker is a stability pattern that monitors failure rates for an external dependency (Neo4j, OpenAI, vector DB). When failures exceed a threshold, the circuit "opens" — requests fail fast without calling the dependency, giving it time to recover. States: CLOSED (normal, count failures) → OPEN (fail all requests, wait timeout) → HALF_OPEN (allow one request to test recovery) → CLOSED if successful. For GraphRAG: OpenAI rate limits (429), Neo4j connection timeouts, vector DB overload — all can cascade: if graph traversal hangs at 30 seconds, all queued requests pile up, API pods exhaust threads, entire system falls over. Circuit breaker: after 5 Neo4j timeouts in 10 seconds → OPEN → all graph queries fail-fast in < 1ms → API pods stay responsive → serve degraded (cached) responses → Neo4j recovers → circuit closes. Without circuit breakers: one failing service can take down the entire GraphRAG system. With them: graceful degradation preserving service availability.

**Q5: How do you achieve zero-downtime deployments for a GraphRAG system with a large graph database?**
> **Answer:** Multi-step zero-downtime deployment strategy: (1) **Blue-green for API layer**: Run two identical API pod sets (Blue: current, Green: new). Deploy new code to Green while Blue serves traffic. Test Green. Switch load balancer to Green. Old Blue kept warm for quick rollback. (2) **Schema migrations for Neo4j**: Never remove/rename existing properties in a single deployment. Use backward-compatible schema: add new property (both old and new code work), deploy new code, backfill old nodes, deprecated old property in next deployment. (3) **Index changes**: New Neo4j indexes are built in background — add index, wait for population (may take minutes for large graphs), then deploy code that uses new index. (4) **Cache invalidation**: On deployment, cache still has valid data. Only invalidate cache if schema changes mean cached data is incompatible. Otherwise, warm cache on new pods while old pods still serve. (5) **Read replica priority**: New code deployed to replicas first (read-only behavior), validate, then switch primary. (6) **Rollback**: Keep graph snapshots (Neo4j backup) at each deployment. If critical failure, restore from snapshot + redeploy old code.

### D. System Design Question

**Design a Production GraphRAG System Serving 50,000 Concurrent Users**

```
ASSUMPTIONS:
  - 50,000 concurrent users
  - 500K queries/hour (peak)
  - P95 latency target: < 2 seconds
  - 99.9% availability
  - Graph: 100M entities, 1B relationships

CAPACITY PLANNING:

API LAYER:
  Each FastAPI pod: handles 500 concurrent requests
  With P95 latency 2s: ~250 requests/second throughput per pod
  Needed throughput: 500K/hour = 139 req/s → 1 pod (insufficient for bursts)
  Target: 10 pods → 2,500 req/s capacity (10x headroom for bursts)
  Auto-scaling: 5-20 pods based on CPU and request queue depth

NEO4J:
  Traversal queries: 70% of 500K = 350K/hour = 97 queries/second
  Expected cache hit rate: 70% → ~29 queries/second hit Neo4j
  Neo4j read replica: handles ~500 queries/second
  Needed: 1 primary + 2 read replicas (HA)
  With sharding: 3 domain shards × 3-node cluster = 9 Neo4j instances

REDIS CLUSTER:
  Cache size: 1M entity neighborhoods × 5KB avg = 5GB
  Redis Cluster: 3 shards × 2 replicas = 6 nodes
  Memory per shard: 16GB
  Hit rate target: 70%+ (reduces Neo4j load)

LLM (Azure OpenAI):
  500K queries × 1000 tokens avg = 500M tokens/hour
  PTU (provisioned throughput): 100K TPM = 6M tokens/hour
  Need: ~84 PTU units (for peak; use auto-scaling endpoint for overflow)
  Cost estimate: $25,000/month for provisioned throughput

TOTAL INFRA COST ESTIMATE:
  Neo4j: $15,000/month (Enterprise)
  Redis: $3,000/month
  Vector DB (Pinecone): $5,000/month
  LLM (Azure OpenAI): $25,000/month
  Compute (API pods): $2,000/month
  Monitoring/Tracing: $1,000/month
  TOTAL: ~$51,000/month for 50K concurrent users
  Per-query cost: ~$0.10/query
```
